title: Mimamsa (ritual as meaning)
hook: eat your spinach, the sailor got strong: Mimamsa's rule for the stories that sit beside a command

segments.voice: Yesterday Mimamsa rested everything on words with no author: apaurusheya, and a bond of word and meaning nobody invented. Which handed-down line did you say with full attention? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-one.

Eat your spinach. The kid at the table pushes it around the plate. So the parent tries again. You know the cartoon sailor? One can of spinach and he could lift a ship. The kid looks at the spinach differently now. Notice what just happened. The story about the sailor isn't a history lesson. Nobody's checking whether sailors really work that way. The story is there for one reason: to make the instruction land. Mimamsa found the Veda doing the same thing, and it made a rule about it. Today, on our last day with Mimamsa, we learn how it reads.
screen: `EAT YOUR SPINACH.` → `THE CARTOON SAILOR.` → `THE STORY SERVES THE COMMAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the problem Jaimini faced. Mimamsa says the Veda is about dharma, what is to be done. But parts of the Veda don't tell anyone to do anything. It praises, it explains, it tells stories about the gods. So in the second section of his first book, Jaimini lets an objector speak. If the Veda's purpose is action, the objector says, these passages that ask for nothing have no purpose at all. Shabara's commentary gives an example the objector might point to, a passage that simply tells of a god who wept. Jaimini's answer is the rule. These passages, called arthavada, belong together with the injunctions they stand beside. They have a purpose: they praise the act that's being asked for. They are the sailor and his spinach. A story about the gods, set next to a command, makes the command shine. And so, in Jaimini's answer, these passages aren't wasted. They help the asking. This is one more sense of our title, ritual as meaning. Mimamsa reads everything, even the stories, as pointing to something done. Now look back on the week. The desire to know dharma. Dharma heard in injunction, not seen by the eye. Apurva carrying the act to its fruit. Words with no author. And today, stories in the service of the doing. Tomorrow, a school reads many of the same texts with a different question in mind, and we'll hear it on its own terms.
screen: `PASSAGES THAT ASK FOR NOTHING.` · `ARTHAVADA PRAISES THE ACT.` · `NO LINE IS WASTED.` · `EVEN STORIES POINT TO DOING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let the act be the meaning for two minutes. Sit, and let your breath settle. Choose one plain action: bringing your palms together, then laying them open on your knees, or bowing your head a little and raising it again. Do it once, carefully, in order, with full attention. Rest. Then do it again, exactly the same way. Don't explain it to yourself. Let the doing be enough. If you pray, you can make that small movement your offering. The bell holds the time.
Mimamsa. The school that reads the Veda as instruction, where even the stories, arthavada, are there to praise the act that's asked for.

Your line: Mimamsa, ritual as meaning. Today, choose one ordinary act, washing a cup, lighting a lamp, tying a shoe, and do it with full attention, in order, as if it were asked of you. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: Mimamsa readers sort the Veda into injunctions and supporting passages, arthavada, and read the praise and stories as serving the acts they stand beside, so that these passages have a purpose.

fork.setup: you're reading the Veda as a student of Mimamsa, and you reach a passage that just tells of a god who wept. it asks nothing. what is it for?
